unitDescription.value:
In this 8-week unit, students explore interior design through a human-centred design approach within the built environments context. They investigate how people experience and interact with interior spaces, considering client needs, ergonomics, accessibility, spatial planning, movement and aesthetic principles. Students analyse existing interiors to identify how layout, scale, proportion, lighting, colour, furniture and visual style can influence the function, comfort and experience of a space. Virtual reality (VR) is used as an immersive design tool, allowing students to experience spaces at 1:1 scale and evaluate how effectively design decisions respond to the needs of users.

Applying an iterative design process, students develop an interior environment in response to a simulated client brief. They explore the client's needs and preferences, establish design criteria, generate alternative spatial concepts and progressively refine their preferred solution. Using 3D modelling and visualisation software, students create and test their interior design through virtual walkthroughs, using feedback and observations to improve spatial layout, usability and aesthetic qualities. The unit culminates in a digital presentation and 1:1 scale VR walkthrough in which students communicate their design process, justify key interior design decisions and evaluate how effectively their solution responds to the client and identified success criteria.

cohortAndClassConsiderations.value:
The Year 10 cohort at St Brendan's College comprises day and boarding students from diverse regional, rural, and remote backgrounds, presenting a wide range of prior experience with digital technologies, CAD software, and spatial representation. Learning experiences are structured to support varying levels of digital literacy and technical spatial visualization through scaffolded software tutorials, step-by-step 3D modelling guides, and structured design folio templates.

To accommodate diverse learning needs, explicit instruction in architectural scale, ergonomic standards, and technical vocabulary is embedded alongside visual and practical exemplars. Extension strategies challenge proficient students to incorporate complex spatial layouts, advanced lighting/material rendering, and detailed environmental lifecycle analyses. 

Practical implementation of virtual reality (VR) technologies requires clear classroom management protocols, including established play boundaries (guardian zones) to manage physical space safety, rotation schedules for Meta Quest 3S hardware usage, and alternative 2D/3D desktop visualisation workflows for students experiencing motion sensitivity. Explicit routines for hardware maintenance, digital file management, and peer collaboration ensure safe, efficient, and inclusive participation across all practical learning experiences.

description.value:
Task Type: Design Project (Folio + VR Prototype + Client Presentation)

Scenario: Students are commissioned to redesign a specific, constrained interior space for a distinct client persona. The design must respond to the client’s functional needs, preferences, accessibility requirements and intended use of the space.

Part 1: The Design Folio (Investigating & Generating)

Client and Space Analysis: Students interpret the client brief and investigate the needs, preferences and behaviours of the user, alongside the functional and spatial constraints of the room.

Ideation: Students develop mood boards, annotated sketches, 2D floor plans and alternative layout concepts that explore spatial organisation, furniture placement, lighting, colour and overall visual style.

Design Development: Students establish success criteria and refine a preferred concept using feedback, ergonomic considerations and human-centred design principles.

Part 2: The Immersive Prototype (Producing)

Virtual Prototype: Using Home Design 3D VR/VisualizeR on the Meta Quest 3S, students construct a 1:1 scale virtual prototype of their interior design.

Iterative Testing: Students experience and test their design in VR, evaluating movement, scale, accessibility, furniture placement and the overall experience of the space. They document at least two significant refinements made as a result of testing and feedback.

Part 3: The Client Walkthrough (Evaluating)

Client Presentation: Students deliver a live or recorded walkthrough of their completed virtual interior.

Justification and Evaluation: Students explain and justify key design decisions and evaluate their final solution against the identified success criteria. They demonstrate how the final design responds to the client’s needs and explain how testing and refinement improved the functionality, usability and overall experience of the space.

conditions.value:
• Folio: 4–6 A3 pages (or digital equivalent) of annotated design thinking, including mood boards, scaled 2D spatial layouts, material lifecycle analyses, and iterative VR testing documentation.
• Prototype: Functional, fully rendered 1:1 scale virtual interior environment developed using specialised 3D modelling and VR software.
• Pitch: 3–5 minute multimodal recorded or live walkthrough defending spatial, aesthetic, and material choices against the design criteria.
• Duration and supervision: Completed over 5–6 weeks of integrated class time under teacher direction and monitoring, with independent development as required.

achievementStandard.value: By the end of Year 10 students explain how people consider factors that impact on design decisions and the technologies used to design and produce products, services and environments for sustainable living. They explain the contribution of innovation, enterprise skills and emerging technologies to global preferred futures. For one or more of the technologies contexts, students explain the features of technologies and their appropriateness for purpose, and create designed solutions based on an analysis of needs or opportunities. Students create, adapt and refine design ideas, processes and solutions and justify their decisions against developed design criteria that include sustainability. They communicate design ideas, processes and solutions to a range of audiences, including using digital tools. Students independently and collaboratively develop and apply production and project management plans, adjusting processes when necessary. They select and use technologies skilfully and safely to produce designed solutions.

moderation.value:
Internal moderation is conducted systematically across the faculty to ensure consistency of teacher judgement against the Australian Curriculum Year 9–10 Design and Technologies achievement standards. This process includes:

*   **Standardisation (Pre-assessment):** Prior to task delivery, teachers collaboratively review the task brief, Guide to Making Judgements (GTMJ), and sample VR design folios. Benchmarks are established to ensure a common understanding of evidence required for spatial flow analysis, material lifecycle evaluations, and iterative prototyping across performance levels (A–E).
*   **Monitoring (Week 6):** Intermediate benchmarking of draft design folios (needs analysis, mood boards, and 2D floor plans) and initial 3D spatial models. Faculty members calibrate feedback to confirm that student evidence accurately documents VR testing and iterative design decisions.
*   **Moderation Conferencing (Week 9–10):** Teachers collaboratively review recorded VR walkthroughs, pitches, and completed design folios at key grade boundaries (A/B, B/C, C/D). Judgements regarding the justification of interior design choices and technical execution are calibrated against the achievement standard.
*   **Cross-Marking:** Blind cross-marking of a representative cohort sample (high, medium, low, and borderline responses) is conducted to ensure objectivity, equity, and consistency in grading standards across all classes. Selected exemplar work is archived to support future benchmarking.

keyTeachingExperiences.value: Students commence the unit with an induction into the design brief and the fundamentals of human-centred interior architecture across three lessons. Across the week, students unpack how spatial planning, accessibility, and ergonomic standards impact occupant wellbeing, explore how virtual reality functions as an architectural visualisation tool, and establish strict workshop safety routines. The week concludes with physical hardware inductions, mapping physical boundaries and calibrating the Meta Quest 3S headsets.

resources.value: Meta Quest 3S headsets and controllers, equipment sanitisation wipes, boundary safety markers/floor tape, Assessment Brief: 'The Virtual Pitch', Part 1 Design Folio digital template, tape measures, Australian Standards (AS 1428.1) accessibility summary guides.

theory.value: Explicit instruction introduces human-centred design principles within the built environment, defining how spatial planning, anthropometric clearances, and universal accessibility directly influence user comfort and physical wellbeing. Students investigate the role of emerging virtual reality (VR) technologies as rapid prototyping and 1:1 scale visualisation tools, analysing how immersive environments overcome the spatial distortion common to conventional 2D orthographic projections. Explicit teaching details workplace health and safety (WHS) protocols for immersive technology, focusing on physical obstacle avoidance, boundary configuration (guardian zones), device sanitisation, and strategies to manage cyber-sickness or perceptual disorientation. Architectural scale, sightline awareness, and foundational design terminology are formally defined to prepare students for technical drawing and spatial analysis.

prac.value: Students complete a structured hardware onboarding process within designated workshop bays using the Meta Quest 3S headsets. Working in pairs, students map out physical room-scale boundaries (guardian zones), calibrate head straps and interpupillary distance (IPD) settings, and navigate basic spatial menus. In a desktop investigation, students conduct an ergonomic audit of their immediate learning space, using tape measures and scale rules to record door clearances, desk clearances, and circulation paths against standard accessibility benchmarks. Findings and spatial observations are collated in the introductory section of their Part 1 Design Folio.

assessment.value: Formative: Teacher observation checklist assessing compliance with WHS protocols, guardian zone calibration, and safe operational handling of VR hardware. Informal questioning assessing comprehension of human-centred design principles.

activities.title: Core Vocabulary: Human-Centred Built Environments
activities.teacherDoes: Welcome Year 9/10 Design and Technologies. Today we commence our unit 'The Virtual Pitch' by establishing four core architectural principles on the board. Look at our first term: Human-Centred Design (HCD). When architects plan an interior, they do not start with wall paint or decorative fittings; they start with the human occupant. For example, if designing an educational study hub, an HCD approach begins by studying how a student sits, reads, and navigates the space over a two-hour study session. Next is Ergonomics—the quantitative science of anthropometry, matching furniture heights and clearances to 5th–95th percentile human dimensions. Third, Universal Accessibility mandates that environments accommodate people of all physical capabilities without requiring segregation or specialised adaptations, aligned with Australian Standard AS 1428.1. Finally, Spatial Planning is the strategic zoning of functional areas, acoustic buffers, and circulation routes. Let us record these definitions into our workbook.
activities.studentsDo: Read the term bank and write the matching definition alongside each locked architectural term in the workbook table.
activities.visibleInstructions: Examine the four architectural terms in the table. Match each term to its precise definition from the bank provided.
activities.questioning:
Why must interior architects prioritise anthropometric ergonomics before selecting aesthetic finishes? Expected: Aesthetic styling cannot compensate for a dysfunctional layout where desk clearances cause musculoskeletal strain or corridors restrict mobility.
How does universal accessibility ensure social equity in built environments? Expected: Designing for universal accessibility ensures all occupants, regardless of physical ability or age, can enter, navigate, and participate without special adaptations or loss of dignity.
What is the functional difference between spatial planning and ergonomics? Expected: Spatial planning manages macro room layouts, zoning, and circulation paths, whereas ergonomics focuses on the micro physical interactions between the human body and specific furniture or equipment.
activities.scaffolding:
Core Definitions Reference:
- Human-Centred Design (HCD): A design methodology prioritising the physical, emotional, and functional needs of human occupants over purely aesthetic or structural considerations.
- Ergonomics: The applied science of designing equipment, furniture, and layouts to fit human body dimensions, posture, and natural movement patterns.
- Universal Accessibility: Designing built spaces, pathways, and products so they are fully usable by all people without need for specialised adaptation (AS 1428.1).
- Spatial Planning: The strategic arrangement of physical forms, functional zones, and circulation paths within an interior footprint.
activities.eLearning: Display the four core terms and definition bank on the interactive whiteboard while students complete their paper workbook table.
activities.transition: Now that we have established our core vocabulary, let us deconstruct our client brief for 'The Virtual Pitch' to identify our design constraints.

activities.title: Deconstructing 'The Virtual Pitch' Assessment Brief
activities.teacherDoes: Direct attention to the front display where 'The Virtual Pitch' assessment task sheet is projected. Let us deconstruct our assessment deliverables and criteria. The task is divided into three distinct phases across the term. In Part 1, you will develop an Investigating and Generating Design Folio, documenting your client persona, spatial zoning diagrams, and ergonomic clearances. For example, if your client is a coastal marine researcher, your folio must establish clear bench heights and circulation corridors. In Part 2, you will step beyond traditional 2D CAD models and construct an immersive prototype at 1:1 scale using our Meta Quest 3S headsets. This allows you to experience real sightlines and reach envelopes. While testing in VR, you must assess accessibility against AS 1428.1 and document at least two iterative design refinements based on user feedback. In Part 3, you will deliver a multimodal client walkthrough pitch defending your architectural decisions. Record these key milestones into your guided notes.

activities.questioning:
Why does this assessment require building an immersive prototype at 1:1 scale in VR rather than relying solely on 2D orthographic floor plans? Expected: 2D floor plans can mask vertical clearances, reach distances, and perceived spatial claustrophobia, whereas 1:1 scale VR reveals true human sightlines and physical proportions.
What form of evidence must be documented during the Part 2 testing phase to meet the highest achievement standard? Expected: Documenting at least two iterative design refinements supported by VR testing observations and accessibility compliance notes.
How does defining client constraints early in the Design Folio protect a project from scope creep? Expected: Clear persona parameters establish measurable criteria for spatial needs, budget, and materials, ensuring all generated concepts directly address user requirements.

activities.title: Client Persona Analysis: Spatial & Ergonomic Constraints
activities.teacherDoes: Project the client persona on the board: 'Arthur, a 72-year-old retired marine biologist living on the Capricorn Coast. Arthur has restricted knee flexion and relies on a walking cane, requires high task lighting for reading nautical charts due to early macular degeneration, and needs generous corridor clearances.' Let us model how an interior architect deconstructs this profile into three architectural categories. First, user physical and sensory challenges: Arthur has reduced joint mobility, fall risks, and decreased visual acuity. Second, we convert these challenges into geometric constraints: a standard 900mm domestic hallway is inadequate because Arthur's cane adds 200mm to his lateral width, so we require a minimum 1000mm to 1200mm clear path and a 1500mm turning circle. Third, design solutions: we specify flush floor transitions without trip steps, lever handles instead of knobs, and 500-lux directional task lighting. Now, synthesise Arthur's profile in your workbook across these three areas.
activities.studentsDo: Read Arthur's client persona profile and complete the three structured written response sections in the workbook, translating user needs into architectural solutions.
activities.visibleInstructions: Review Arthur's client profile. In your workbook, document his physical/sensory challenges, establish specific geometric constraints in millimetres, and propose concrete architectural solutions.
activities.questioning:
How does Arthur's reliance on a walking cane alter the minimum clearance requirement for circulation corridors? Expected: Standard 900mm domestic corridors are insufficient; clearances must expand to at least 1000mm to 1200mm to allow cane placement and side clearance without scraping walls or bumping knuckles.
Why is lighting considered an ergonomic factor alongside furniture dimensions in architectural design? Expected: Ergonomics encompasses sensory comfort; inadequate lux levels cause eye strain, fatigue, and serious trip hazards for visually impaired occupants.
What joinery design modification would assist a client with limited knee flexion when accessing low storage? Expected: Raising base cabinetry kickboards and installing pull-out pantry drawers between 450mm and 1200mm height to eliminate the need for deep squatting.
activities.scaffolding:
Analysis Framework:
1. User Physical & Sensory Challenges:
   - Mobility: Restricted knee flexion, cane usage, reduced stride length.
   - Sensory: Reduced visual contrast acuity requiring elevated illumination.
2. Geometric Layout Constraints:
   - Hallway circulation: Minimum 1000mm–1200mm clear width.
   - Turning clearance: 1540mm diameter unobstructed circular space.
   - Reach envelope: Active vertical reach band between 450mm and 1200mm above finished floor level.
3. Built-Environment Design Solutions:
   - Flush threshold transitions (no steps/raised sills).
   - Lever door handles (AS 1428.1 compliant) and D-pull drawer hardware.
   - Dedicated high-lux (500 lux) task lighting and matte non-reflective, non-slip floor finishes.

lessons.title: Ergonomics & Spatial Accessibility Audit
lessons.learningGoal: Measure physical layout clearances and evaluate spatial layouts against standard Australian accessibility benchmarks (AS 1428.1).

orientate.smartStart: A projected floor plan shows a classroom door opening measuring 760mm wide. Students have 3 minutes to determine whether this opening meets standard wheelchair accessibility guidelines and calculate the clearance shortfall.
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can measure physical clearances in our classroom and evaluate them against Australian accessibility benchmarks

activities.title: Modelled Architectural Measurement Protocols
activities.teacherDoes: Gather around the classroom doorway for a practical demonstration of architectural measurement protocols under AS 1428.1. Notice how amateur draftsmen often measure door frames from jamb to jamb—this is incorrect. Model placing the end of the steel tape measure firmly against the inner face of the open door leaf and measuring across to the opposing door stop. The true clear opening must be a minimum of 850mm. Next, demonstrate measuring circulation corridors between the outermost protrusions—such as skirting boards or door handles, not bare masonry walls—requiring at least 1000mm continuous width. Then, measure desk clearance from the finished floor to the underside of the desk frame, showing that 700mm vertical and 800mm horizontal clearance are required for knee comfort and wheelchair access. Finally, demonstrate laying out a 1540mm diameter circle on the floor to verify turning space. Observe each callout on the projected diagram and record the standard benchmark dimension and rule.
activities.studentsDo: Observe the physical measurement demonstration, note the measurement rules for clear openings and obstacles, and annotate the four callouts on the workbook diagram.
activities.visibleInstructions: Watch the teacher measurement demonstration. For each numbered callout on your workbook diagram, record the AS 1428.1 standard dimension and the exact measurement rule.
activities.questioning:
Why must the clear opening of a doorway be measured from the face of the open door leaf to the opposing door stop rather than between the jambs? Expected: The thickness of the open door leaf protrudes into the door opening, reducing the actual usable clearance for an occupant or wheelchair.
What hazard arises if an architect designs circulation pathways based on wall-to-wall dimensions rather than skirting-to-skirting clearances? Expected: Furniture, skirtings, door handles, and wall fixtures protrude into the space, creating pinch points that reduce width below the mandatory 1000mm standard.
Why does AS 1428.1 specify 700mm vertical clearance beneath work surfaces? Expected: To allow adequate clearance for wheelchair armrests and occupant thighs without contact or postural compression.
activities.scaffolding:
AS 1428.1 Standard Benchmarks Reference:
- Callout 1 (Door clear opening): Min 850mm clear width (measured from face of open door at 90 degrees to door stop).
- Callout 2 (Continuous circulation path): Min 1000mm clear unobstructed width.
- Callout 3 (Seated knee clearance): Min 700mm vertical height from floor to underside of table/desk frame; min 800mm width.
- Callout 4 (Wheelchair turning space): Min 1540mm diameter circular unobstructed floor space.

activities.title: Guided Circulation Pathway & Entryway Audit
activities.teacherDoes: Pair students up and issue each pair with a 5m heavy-duty steel tape measure. Direct pairs to four designated measurement zones across the design studio: Zone A (entry door), Zone B (main hallway circulation corridor), Zone C (demonstration desk knee clearance), and Zone D (communal turning zone near the materials store). Circulate actively, checking that students keep their tapes taut and level without sagging. Intervene to demonstrate reading metric millimetres accurately rather than rounding to centimetres. Show students how to record the actual dimension and evaluate compliance against the AS 1428.1 benchmark.
activities.studentsDo: Work in assigned pairs to measure the four designated classroom zones using tape measures, record millimeter dimensions, and determine compliance status.
activities.visibleInstructions: Collaborate with your partner to measure the four assigned architectural elements. Record the exact measurement in millimetres and evaluate compliance against the AS 1428.1 benchmark.
activities.questioning:
If our main circulation corridor measures 1150mm wide with student bags placed on the floor, is it compliant in practice? Expected: Non-compliant in practice, because floor clutter reduces the clear continuous travel path below the mandatory 1000mm width.
Why does Australian Standard AS 1428.1 require a 1540mm circular space rather than a square box for turning? Expected: Wheelchairs require a circular sweeping radius to rotate 360 degrees without their footrests or rear wheels colliding with corners.
How should a designer resolve an entryway that measures only 820mm clear opening? Expected: Specify an offset pivot hinge, install an 870mm/920mm door leaf, or replace the swing door with an unobstructed cavity slider.
activities.scaffolding:
Measurement Protocol Checklist:
1. Hook tape firmly against the baseline surface.
2. Keep tape taut, level, and perpendicular to opposing surfaces.
3. Measure between the narrowest physical points (e.g. skirting to skirting, door face to door stop).
4. Record all values in millimetres (mm).
5. Pass = Measurement meets or exceeds the minimum benchmark; Fail = Measurement is below the benchmark.

activities.title: Individual Workstation Ergonomic Compliance Audit
activities.teacherDoes: Circulate around the studio as students perform an independent ergonomic audit of their personal workstations. Model how to measure seat pan height from the floor to the top of the seat cushion, and check thigh angle—thighs should be horizontal with feet flat on the floor (typically 400mm–500mm). Check desk depth and width (minimum 900mm wide by 600mm deep). Prompt students to identify any pinch points or ergonomic hazards in their seating posture and record recommendations in their Design Folio.

activities.visibleInstructions: Conduct an independent audit of your personal workstation. Measure each feature, check compliance against the ergonomic criteria, and tick each compliant item.
activities.questioning:

Why should the primary work surface allow at least 900mm width and 600mm depth? Expected: It accommodates computer hardware, keyboard, writing materials, and forearm support without awkward shoulder abduction or reaching strain.
What ergonomic adjustment should be made if a student's feet cannot rest flat on the floor at the required desk height? Expected: Provide an adjustable angled footrest so the student's thighs remain horizontal while supporting the feet.

activities.title: Hardware Anatomy & Calibration Sequence
activities.teacherDoes: Direct student attention to the teacher demonstration workbench where the Meta Quest 3S hardware is displayed. Model the four mandatory stages of the hardware calibration sequence. First, show how to sanitise the facial silicone interface using antibacterial wipes and clean the optical pancake lenses using only a dry microfiber cloth—never liquid chemicals. Second, model fitting the headset: loosen the top strap and side tensioners completely, position the visor firmly against the brow and cheekbones, and gently tighten the side straps equally before securing the top strap so the weight is distributed across the cranium. Third, explain Interpupillary Distance (IPD): demonstrate toggling the three-position lens slider (58mm, 63mm, 68mm) while looking at calibration text until chromatic aberration disappears. Explain that incorrect IPD causes optical convergence errors and severe cyber-sickness. Fourth, show how double-tapping the headset chassis toggles high-resolution passthrough video to verify physical spatial awareness. Walk through each stage on the flow diagram.
activities.studentsDo: Observe the teacher demonstration of the Meta Quest 3S hardware calibration sequence, take structured notes, and complete the four stages of the flow diagram in the workbook.
activities.visibleInstructions: Observe the modelled Quest 3S setup sequence. Record the critical procedural step and safety rule for each of the four sequential calibration stages in your workbook flow diagram.
activities.questioning:
Why is precise adjustment of the Interpupillary Distance (IPD) slider essential before beginning any virtual walkthrough? Expected: If the lenses do not align with the user's pupil centres, the eyes must constantly strain to converge the stereoscopic images, causing eye fatigue, headaches, and vestibular nausea.
How do the pass-through tracking cameras contribute to workplace health and safety in an architectural workshop? Expected: Pass-through cameras allow the user to see their real physical environment instantly without removing the headset, avoiding collisions with peers and physical equipment.
Why should liquid cleaning sprays or paper towels never be applied to VR optical lenses? Expected: Chemical sprays erode anti-reflective lens coatings and paper fibres scratch the delicate optical plastic surfaces, causing permanent visual distortion.
activities.scaffolding:
Meta Quest 3S Calibration Stages:
1. Sanitise & Inspect: Wipe silicone facial cushion with disinfectant wipe; clean lenses using dry microfiber cloth only.
2. Ergonomic Fit: Loosen all straps, cup back of head with rear strap, tension side straps evenly, then fasten top strap.
3. IPD Calibration: Set lens spacing slider to Position 1 (58mm), 2 (63mm), or 3 (68mm) until calibration text is crisp.
4. Passthrough Verification: Double-tap headset side to activate passthrough; confirm room boundary clarity and tracking stability.

activities.title: Deconstructing Brief Parameters
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly model how to deconstruct an architectural brief on the projector. Demonstrate categorising statements into non-negotiable architectural constraints, client functional needs, and flexible aesthetic preferences using a sample apartment brief: 'Notice this statement: External load-bearing masonry walls and window locations cannot be structurally modified. Can we move this wall if we need more floor area? No, because it provides structural support and building envelope integrity. Therefore, we classify this as a Hard Architectural Constraint. The design implication is that all circulation paths and fixed joinery must be planned within this fixed perimeter envelope. Next, look at: Client requires continuous unhindered mobility for walking cane and occasional wheelchair transit. This is a Mandatory Functional Need rooted in human ergonomics and accessibility. The concrete architectural design implication is non-negotiable: pathways must maintain a minimum 1000mm clear width and turning circles must reach 1540mm to comply with AS 1428.1.' Model how each brief parameter dictates specific spatial layout and clearance decisions.
activities.studentsDo: Follow the teacher demonstration on the screen, examine the categorisation methodology, and complete the classification and design implication columns in the workbook table.
activities.visibleInstructions: Review the modelled brief breakdown on the projector. Classify each brief statement into its operational category and record the concrete architectural design implication in your workbook table.
activities.questioning:
Why must an architectural perimeter wall be classified as a hard constraint rather than a preference?
Expected: A structural perimeter wall cannot be relocated without structural alterations and engineering approvals, whereas interior furniture layouts can be freely adapted.
How does a client mobility requirement alter spatial planning in a domestic interior?
Expected: It dictates non-negotiable minimum clearance widths for circulation corridors and doorway thresholds in accordance with AS 1428.1 accessibility standards.
What is the risk of treating an aesthetic preference as a mandatory functional constraint?
Expected: It unnecessarily restricts spatial problem-solving and may compromise essential ergonomic or accessibility requirements to satisfy a flexible styling choice.
activities.scaffolding:
Classification Categories:
- Hard Architectural Constraint: A fixed physical, structural, or legal boundary (e.g. load-bearing masonry walls, window penetrations, plumbing risers, ceiling heights).
- Mandatory Functional Need: A practical requirement essential for occupant safety, daily task routines, and mobility (e.g. wheelchair turning circles, desk work heights, reach zones).
- Aesthetic Preference: A flexible stylistic choice that can be adapted without compromising function (e.g. timber species, colour tone, textile weave, decorative luminaires).

activities.title: Client Persona User Story Extraction
activities.teacherDoes: Guide the class through translating client profile statements into formal user story syntax (As a... I want... So that...). Co-construct a comprehensive user story based on the client persona, emphasising how the 'so that' clause justifies spatial dimensions and functional features: 'Look at our persona profile: Arthur is a remote consultant who uses a walking cane and conducts daily client meetings. For the role stem, we establish: As a professional working remotely with limited physical mobility. For the want stem, we specify concrete architectural features: I want an ergonomically zoned workspace with continuous 1000mm pathway clearances and dedicated acoustic absorption. Finally, the crucial justification stem: So that I can navigate safely without trip hazards and conduct professional video conferences without acoustic echo. Notice how the so that clause proves to the client why the spatial allocation and acoustic materials are essential.'

activities.questioning:
What risk occurs if an architectural designer omits the 'so that' clause in project requirements?
Expected: The team might implement a costly spatial feature without understanding the underlying functional reason, risking an ineffective layout.
How does defining the client role protect against personal designer bias?
Expected: It anchors design choices directly to user needs, ergonomics, and daily routines rather than the designer's personal tastes.
Why must the 'I want' clause specify measurable physical features rather than vague desires?
Expected: Measurable features like 1000mm clearances and acoustic wall panels can be verified in CAD drawings and 1:1 VR models.

activities.title: Core Architectural Typologies & Material Terminology
activities.teacherDoes: Present visual exemplars of contemporary residential interior typologies on the projector. Explicitly define key terminology including Biophilic Design, Acoustic Reverberation, Task Lighting, and Colour Temperature (Kelvin): 'Look at this exemplar apartment: if we specify floor-to-ceiling glass and hard tiled flooring, sound waves reflect repeatedly between parallel hard surfaces. That persistence of sound energy is Acoustic Reverberation. To mitigate this echo without altering structural walls, an architect installs slotted timber battens with porous polyester backing. This not only absorbs sound energy but also introduces natural wood grain and daylight reflection, directly fulfilling Biophilic Design principles.' activities.questioning:
How does surface materiality influence acoustic comfort in an open-plan room?
Expected: Hard reflective surfaces like polished concrete and glass reflect sound waves, causing high reverberation and echo, whereas porous textiles and slotted timber battens absorb sound energy.
Why would an interior architect specify 3000K warm white lighting over 5000K cool white for a domestic living zone?

activities.title: Core Vocabulary of Spatial Planning
activities.teacherDoes: Introduce core spatial planning terms on the projector: Adjacency Matrix, Bubble Diagram, Circulation Path, and Functional Zoning. An architect uses a structured grid to evaluate physical or acoustic closeness before drawing walls. For example, in our Keppel Bay Marina workspace, we position reception adjacent to the entry, but keep private workstations separated from noisy amenities to prevent acoustic clashes.' Expected: Incompatible zones such as quiet focus pods and noisy amenities may end up adjacent, creating acoustic conflicts that are difficult and expensive to remediate.

- Bubble Diagram: A non-scaled conceptual schematic using circular shapes to explore spatial relationships, relative volume, and access.
- Circulation Path: The continuous physical travel route taken by occupants through an interior, categorised as primary or secondary.
- Functional Zoning: The strategic division of an interior floor plan into distinct activity sectors such as public, private, or service areas.

Expected: A Secondary ('S') rating because staff and clients require convenient access during breaks, but direct open doorways would cause acoustic and olfactory disturbances.
Why must the Workstation Hub have a Non-adjacent ('N') rating with the main public entry?
Expected: To protect confidential client data on computer screens, reduce foot-traffic distractions, and maintain acoustic privacy.
activities.scaffolding:
Coding Standards:
- Primary (P): Direct physical connection or immediate open doorway access.
- Secondary (S): Accessible via shared circulation hallway or buffered zone.
- Non-adjacent (N): Acoustically and visually isolated by partition walls.

activities.title: Generative Bubble Diagramming
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate on the document camera how to convert the matrix grid into a graphic bubble diagram. Delivery script: 'Notice how I draw the Workstation Hub bubble twice the size of the Meeting Room, while Amenities Bay is a compact circle. Next, look at our matrix codes: Entry to Meeting Room was P, so I connect them with a thick double solid line representing a primary circulation corridor. Entry to Workstation Hub was N, so I place them on opposite sides, separated by a physical buffer. Workstations to Amenities was P, so they connect directly.' How does line weight in a bubble diagram help communicate traffic hierarchy to a client?

Why should bubble sizes vary even though this is a non-scaled drawing?

activities.title: Modelling Architectural Conventions & Scale
activities.teacherDoes: Project a 1:50 drafting template. Model drawing external and partition walls with accurate thickness: 'At 1:50 scale, 100mm in the real world equals 2mm on our drawing paper. Always draw double lines for walls so structural framing and plasterboard are realistically represented.' Demonstrate drafting a 90-degree door swing arc showing leaf travel, drawing thin double-line glazed windows, and using furniture stencils to position desks with anthropometric clearance. Review key Australian clearance standards: 900mm main path, 750mm desk gap, and 1200mm wheelchair turn.
activities.studentsDo: Observe the modelled drafting conventions, note scale conversion rules, and annotate the four technical drawing features on the floor plan diagram in the workbook.
activities.visibleInstructions: Examine the technical drawing slide on the board. Annotate the four architectural features on your workbook diagram with their drafting convention and scale dimension.
activities.questioning:
Why do architects draft the swing of a door as a 90-degree arc rather than just showing an open door leaf?
Expected: The arc visually identifies the entire swept volume of the door leaf, ensuring no furniture, light switches, or pathways encroach on its movement.
What practical problem arises on site if walls are drawn as single hairline strokes without showing wall thickness?
Expected: Real structural timber studs and plasterboard occupy 100mm to 150mm; ignoring wall thickness results in rooms that are smaller than planned, causing planned joinery to fail to fit.
activities.scaffolding:
Conventions at 1:50 Scale:
- Scale Factor: Real dimension (mm) / 50 = Drawing dimension (mm)
- Callout 1: External double-line wall thickness (100mm actual = 2mm on plan)
- Callout 2: Door swing arc (90-degree quarter-circle indicating swept clearance)
- Callout 3: Glazed window opening (thin double lines centred within wall opening)
- Callout 4: Fixed workstation footprint (1600x800mm actual = 32x16mm on plan with 900mm clearance)

activities.title: Guided Clearance & Scale Conversions
activities.teacherDoes: Guide students through converting real-world millimetre clearances into 1:50 scale values. Explicitly explain the ergonomic rationale for each dimension: 900mm for continuous primary pathways, 750mm for secondary chair clearances, and 1200mm for wheelchair turning spaces. Delivery script: 'Take 900mm divided by 50, which gives 18mm on your scale ruler. Next, between two desks, we need 750mm for someone to push back their office chair without bumping into the colleague behind them; 750 divided by 50 equals 15mm. For accessible turning under AS 1428.1, 1200mm divided by 50 gives 24mm.' Model completing the cloze sentences with the class.
activities.studentsDo: Complete the cloze passage in the workbook by calculating and inserting the correct scaled millimetre values and architectural standards.
activities.visibleInstructions: Calculate the 1:50 scale drawing equivalents and complete the missing values in the guided cloze passage in your workbook.

If a real hallway measures 900mm wide, how many millimetres will you measure on your 1:50 layout paper?
Expected: Exactly 18mm (900 divided by 50).
Why is a 600mm gap between two workstations considered an ergonomic failure?
Expected: 600mm is too narrow for comfortable chair push-back and forces occupants to squeeze sideways, violating secondary circulation standards.
activities.scaffolding:
Mathematical Conversion Formula:
- Drawing mm = Actual mm / 50
- 900mm = 18mm on paper
- 750mm = 15mm on paper
- 1200mm = 24mm on paper
- 100mm wall = 2mm on paper

activities.title: The Layout Compliance Audit
activities.teacherDoes: Provide a sample draft 1:50 floor plan in the workbook containing four deliberate layout errors (a corridor pinched to 700mm, a door swing colliding with a desk, an inter-desk gap of 600mm, and an obstructed turning radius). Delivery script: 'Place the zero mark of your 1:50 scale rule on the interior wall edge and measure across the hallway to the desk boundary. If it measures under 18mm, that indicates a violation of our 900mm primary circulation path. Next, measure the circular radius at the reception desk to see if a 24mm diameter wheelchair turning circle fits cleanly.' Circulate the classroom, verifying students' scale rule placement and auditing technique.
activities.studentsDo: Use 1:50 scale rules to measure pathways and clearances on the draft plan, identify the four clearance breaches, and record measurements and corrective actions in the audit table.
activities.visibleInstructions: Using your 1:50 scale rule, measure the clearances on the sample floor plan in your workbook. Identify four layout errors and record your findings and corrective actions in the table.

What specific clearance breach did you discover adjacent to the meeting room entry door?
Expected: The door swing collides with the corner of the reception counter, preventing the door from opening past 60 degrees.
What corrective action would you recommend to resolve an obstructed 1000mm turning circle?

activities.title: Modelling Multi-Criteria Evaluation
activities.teacherDoes: Model the construction of a weighted multi-criteria decision matrix on the projector. Delivery script: 'Designers evaluate spatial options objectively using client-defined criteria. Look at our matrix weightings: Accessibility is 30% because Australian Standard AS 1428.1 compliance is mandatory; Acoustic Zoning and Ergonomics are 25% each; and Daylight Access is 20%. To calculate the weighted score, multiply the raw score out of 5 by the percentage weight divided by 100. For Concept A's Accessibility: 5 multiplied by 0.30 equals 1.50. For Concept B: 3 multiplied by 0.30 equals 0.90.' Demonstrate assigning percentage weightings, computing row totals, and summing composite scores to determine the preferred layout objectively.
activities.studentsDo: Observe the teacher model, record the weighting formula, and complete the sample calculations comparing Concept A and Concept B in the workbook table.
activities.visibleInstructions: Review the projected decision matrix. Note how raw scores are multiplied by percentage weights. Complete the weighted score calculations in your workbook table.
activities.questioning:
Why do architectural designers weight evaluation criteria rather than calculating a simple average score?
Expected: Because mandatory criteria such as life safety and accessibility are critical to project viability, whereas decorative preferences should carry lower relative weighting.
What risk does a designer take if they select a spatial layout based on subjective intuition rather than an objective matrix?
Expected: They risk overlooking critical functional failures, client routine incompatibilities, or compliance breaches that surface during production.
activities.scaffolding:
Mathematical Formula:
- Weighted Score = Raw Score (1 to 5) x (Weight Percentage / 100)
- Total Score = Sum of all weighted category scores
- Highest composite score indicates the preferred layout
activities.eLearning: Projector active with spreadsheet simulation model. Laptops closed.
activities.transition: Now that we have modelled how to compute weighted scores, let us practice evaluating accessibility on a continuum scale.

workbookSpec.title: Weighted Multi-Criteria Decision Matrix
workbookSpec.prompt: Calculate the weighted scores for Concept A and Concept B across each design criterion.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer:
Accessibility (30%): Concept A Raw 5 -> Weighted 1.50; Concept B Raw 3 -> Weighted 0.90.
Acoustic Zoning (25%): Concept A Raw 4 -> Weighted 1.00; Concept B Raw 2 -> Weighted 0.50.
Ergonomics (25%): Concept A Raw 4 -> Weighted 1.00; Concept B Raw 4 -> Weighted 1.00.
Daylight Access (20%): Concept A Raw 4 -> Weighted 0.80; Concept B Raw 5 -> Weighted 1.00.
Total Composite Scores: Concept A = 4.30; Concept B = 3.40.

activities.teacherAnswerKey:
Weighted calculation: Weighted = Raw * (Weight / 100).
1. Accessibility (30%): Concept A Raw 5 -> Weighted 1.50; Concept B Raw 3 -> Weighted 0.90.
2. Acoustic Zoning (25%): Concept A Raw 4 -> Weighted 1.00; Concept B Raw 2 -> Weighted 0.50.
3. Ergonomics (25%): Concept A Raw 4 -> Weighted 1.00; Concept B Raw 4 -> Weighted 1.00.
4. Daylight/Biophilic (20%): Concept A Raw 4 -> Weighted 0.80; Concept B Raw 5 -> Weighted 1.00.
Total Scores: Concept A = 4.30; Concept B = 3.40. Concept A is objectively superior.

activities.title: Formal Selection Justification Writing

Explain how Concept A provides 1000mm accessible corridors and isolates focus desks from public noise. In Section 2, critique Concept B: acknowledge its daylight benefits, but identify why its 750mm corridor pinch point and noisy amenities placement forced its rejection. In Section 3, write your 3-2-1 exit reflection.' Circulate providing sentence-level feedback.

keyTeachingExperiences.value: Students transition from two-dimensional drafting to digital architectural production over three lessons, learning the interface and parametric modelling tools of 3D interior visualisation software. They import and digitise their approved 2D floor plans, extruding external boundary perimeters and internal partition walls to accurate architectural heights and thicknesses. The week concludes with inserting standard architectural fenestrations (doors and windows) and performing initial scale audits via first-person desktop navigation and preliminary VR headset checks.

theory.value: Explicit instruction introduces 3D architectural coordinate systems (X, Y, and Z axes), scale calibration, and parametric modelling workflows within interior visualisation environments. Students examine wall assembly standards, focusing on standard internal wall thicknesses (e.g., 90 mm stud framing with 10 mm plasterboard linings) versus external structural envelopes, ceiling heights (e.g., 2400 mm to 2700 mm), and structural clearances. Lessons explore the parametric placement of architectural fenestrations, detailing standard door opening widths (820 mm to 920 mm for accessible circulation paths) and sill/header heights for natural illumination. The teacher models techniques for navigating 3D space, identifying common digital modelling errors such as unaligned vertices, inverted surface normals, and scale distortion between orthographic views and perspective projections.

prac.value: In the computer lab, students import or reference their approved 2D floor plans to construct the 3D architectural shell, setting grid snaps and entering exact metric dimensions for wall lengths and heights. They erect external perimeters and interior dividing partitions, ensuring all closed geometries form sealed rooms. Students insert architectural elements, selecting and customising door types (hinged, sliding, cavity) and window assemblies to match their Week 3 design drawings. Working in designated software modes, students conduct initial first-person camera walkthroughs and quick Meta Quest 3S boundary checks to verify that room proportions and ceiling volumes translate accurately to 1:1 human perspective without visual distortion.

The red X-axis represents horizontal width from left to right across the ground plane. The green Y-axis controls horizontal depth from front to back. activities.title: Australian Wall and Ceiling Dimension Standards
activities.teacherDoes: Deliver explicit direct instruction using projected technical cross-sections of Australian residential and commercial construction standards. State: 'When modelling in 3D, accuracy begins with real-world wall assemblies. An internal dividing partition consists of a 90 mm timber or light-gauge steel stud, lined on each side with 10 mm plasterboard, giving a total modelled thickness of 110 mm. In contrast, our external structural envelope requires 250 mm to allow for exterior cladding or brick veneer, cavity ventilation, and thermal insulation batts.' Model referencing the National Construction Code (NCC) requirements for vertical clearance: 'The NCC specifies a strict minimum ceiling height of 2400 mm for habitable rooms like living areas and bedrooms, while contemporary architectural designs often specify 2700 mm for enhanced thermal circulation and perceived spatial luxury.'
activities.studentsDo: Listen to the presentation on Australian construction standards and complete the guided cloze passage in the workbook by writing the correct metric values from the word bank into blanks 1 to 4.

activities.questioning:
Why does the National Construction Code mandate a minimum habitable ceiling height of 2400 mm rather than a lower ceiling like 2100 mm?
Expected: To ensure adequate air volume, natural daylight distribution, and occupant psychological well-being, while avoiding claustrophobic spatial compression.

Why do external structural envelopes require more than double the thickness of internal partition walls?
Expected: External envelopes must carry structural building loads, accommodate weatherproofing moisture cavities, and house thermal insulation batts, whereas interior partitions only provide room division and acoustic privacy.
activities.scaffolding:
Key Construction Metric Benchmarks:
- Internal Partition Wall Thickness: 110 mm total (90 mm framing stud + two 10 mm plasterboard linings)
- Internal Framing Stud: 90 mm timber or light-gauge steel
- External Structural Envelope: 250 mm total (brick veneer / cladding + cavity + insulated stud frame)
- NCC Minimum Habitable Ceiling Height: 2400 mm (mandatory for bedrooms and living rooms)
- Standard Contemporary Ceiling Height: 2700 mm (increased volumetric space and daylight)

activities.title: Structural Envelope vs Internal Partition Analysis
activities.teacherDoes: Project a comparative CAD floor plan displaying external structural envelope boundaries alongside lightweight internal partitions. Model evaluating how dimensional discrepancies compound across an interior plan: 'Consider what happens if you inadvertently model internal dividing walls at 250 mm instead of 110 mm. Across three adjacent rooms, you consume 420 mm of usable floor space. A corridor designed at 1100 mm is suddenly squeezed down to 960 mm, breaching the mandatory 1000 mm clear circulation standard under AS 1428.1 for wheelchair access. Conversely, under-sizing external envelopes creates a false impression of spaciousness in VR walkthroughs that collapses when structural framing is introduced.' Direct students to write detailed technical justifications for each section in their workbook.
activities.studentsDo: Compose structured technical justifications in the workbook sections analysing the functional purpose of structural envelopes, the role of internal partitions, and the compounding spatial impacts of incorrect wall thicknesses.
activities.visibleInstructions: In your workbook, complete the three analytical sections: (1) Define the functional role of the structural envelope; (2) Explain the purpose of internal partition walls; (3) Analyse how incorrect wall sizing compromises interior circulation and accessibility compliance.
activities.questioning:
What happens to internal circulation corridors if internal partition walls are accidentally modelled at 250 mm instead of 110 mm?
Expected: Corridors lose up to 140 mm of width per wall, reducing clearances below the mandatory 1000 mm accessibility standard and restricting wheelchair access.

How does maintaining accurate digital wall thickness support client confidence during the Virtual Pitch?
Expected: It guarantees that 1:1 VR walkthroughs accurately reflect physical clearances and structural realities, ensuring the design presented to the client is buildable and code-compliant.
activities.scaffolding:
Analysis Framework:
- Structural Envelope Role: Perimeter boundary enclosure, weatherproofing barrier, load-bearing support, thermal mass and insulation containment (modelled at 250 mm).
- Internal Partition Role: Non-load-bearing room division, visual and acoustic privacy, service cavity reticulation, spatial organisation (modelled at 110 mm).
- Spatial Impacts: Over-thickening constricts corridors below 1000 mm AS 1428.1 compliance, causing door swing clashes; under-thickening miscalculates net lettable area and produces unbuildable door jamb junctions.

workbookSpec.prompt: Analyse the functional roles of structural envelopes and internal partitions, and evaluate the spatial consequences of modelling incorrect wall thicknesses.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer:
Structural Envelope Role: Provides the primary perimeter boundary, structural support, thermal insulation, and weatherproofing for the building shell (modelled at 250 mm).
Internal Partition Role: Subdivides internal volume into distinct functional rooms, provides acoustic privacy, and defines circulation paths without bearing structural loads (modelled at 110 mm).
Impact of Incorrect Wall Sizing on Interior Space: Over-thickening walls reduces usable floor area and narrows corridors below accessibility standards (AS 1428.1); under-thickening walls gives false clearance estimates, misaligns standard door jambs, and compromises realistic fitout planning.

activities.title: Importing and Calibrating 2D Floor Plans
activities.teacherDoes: Open Home Design 3D VR / VisualizeR on the projection screen. Model importing an approved 2D floor plan raster image onto the ground plane. Explain: 'When a digital drawing or image is imported, the software assigns it arbitrary pixel dimensions. If we construct walls immediately, our digital environment will lack true physical scale, making VR testing useless.' Model setting the workspace grid snap to 100 mm to enforce standard modular building increments. Select the software's scale calibration dimension tool, snap crosshairs across a known 3000 mm dimension line from the 2D plan, and enter '3000' in the metric dialogue box. Verify scale accuracy by taking a spot measurement across another verified room boundary, then lock the imported floor plan layer to prevent accidental displacement during extrusion.
activities.studentsDo: Observe the teacher modelling on the projector screen, locate the calibration tools within the software interface, and complete the numbered interface callout annotations in their workbook.
activities.visibleInstructions: Examine the projected software interface diagram in your workbook. Identify the four key calibration tools and record their technical names and operational functions next to callouts 1 to 4.
activities.questioning:
What will happen in VR if you begin constructing walls without calibrating the 2D reference drawing?
Expected: The model will lack a calibrated 1:1 scale, causing rooms, doors, and furniture to feel abnormally giant or miniature in virtual reality.

Why is 100 mm the optimal grid snap setting when laying out major architectural walls?
Expected: It aligns with standard Australian building module increments (e.g. 100 mm, 300 mm, 600 mm) and prevents fractional millimetre misalignments.
activities.scaffolding:
Calibration Sequence & Tool Callouts:
1. Import Reference Tool: Loads the approved 2D floor plan raster/PDF file onto the ground plane layer.
2. Scale Calibration Tool: Establishes real-world 1:1 metric scale by defining the distance between two known reference points.
3. Grid Snap Toggle (100 mm): Constrains digital cursor movement to standard 100 mm architectural modular increments.
4. Layer Lock: Secures the background floor plan image to prevent accidental movement while tracing walls.

activities.title: Parametric Fenestration Insertion Workflow
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate opening the parametric component library in Home Design 3D VR / VisualizeR on the main display. Model selecting standard hinged doors, cavity sliders, and glazed windows. Drag a door component onto a 3D partition wall, showing how the software dynamically subtracts wall geometry. Model adjusting door leaf width to 820 mm (internal) and 920 mm (main entrance), flipping swing direction, and setting window sill heights to 900 mm. State: 'Parametric fenestrations are dynamic objects. Notice how the wall automatically cuts an opening with trim and lintels. If I relocate or delete the door, the wall heals itself seamlessly.' Emphasise how swing direction dictates functional room usability and accessibility compliance.
activities.studentsDo: Observe the demonstration and document the four-step parametric insertion sequence into the workflow diagram in their workbook.

activities.questioning:
Why do parametric doors automatically create wall cutouts, and what happens if you delete the door?
Expected: The parametric component cuts a dynamic boolean opening in the wall; deleting or moving the door causes the wall geometry to heal itself automatically.

Why is door swing orientation critical when designing for accessible circulation?
Expected: Inward swinging doors can trap occupants in small rooms or block emergency egress, while outward swings into narrow corridors obstruct traffic flow.

theory.value: Explicit teaching addresses digital materiality, surface rendering principles, and interior lighting theory within virtual environments. Students explore texture mapping properties—such as diffuse colour, reflectivity, roughness, and bump/normal mapping—analysing how tactile surfaces influence user perception, warmth, and visual weight. Instruction covers layered lighting schemes, distinguishing between ambient (general illumination), task (directed functional lighting), and accent lighting, alongside colour temperature (Kelvin scale) and shadow behaviour. The teacher reinforces strict interior circulation and accessibility benchmarks (such as AS 1428.1 provisions for 900–1000 mm clear corridors and unobstructed furniture clearances) to prevent students overcrowding virtual rooms with decorative assets.

prac.value: Students populate their 3D model using the software's asset library, placing bespoke furniture arrangements, built-in joinery, and plumbing/electrical fixtures aligned with their client's functional brief. They assign realistic materials and textures (e.g., timber grains, brushed metals, fabrics, matte paints) to all internal surfaces, matching the aesthetic palettes formulated in their Week 2 mood boards. Students position and configure light sources, balancing window solar angles with artificial ceiling, task, and accent luminaires to establish mood and visual clarity. Using digital measurement tools, students verify that spatial pathways, door clearances, and seating zones maintain prescribed physical clearances for fluid circulation.

assessment.value: Formative: Peer review and teacher consultation on interior asset layout, material cohesiveness, and compliance with circulation and accessibility clearance standards.

outlineTheme.value: Students fit out their virtual interior spaces by populating them with custom furniture, cabinetry, fixtures, and fittings aligned with client lifestyle requirements. They apply materials, textures, and artificial and natural lighting solutions to reinforce the aesthetic theme and enhance spatial atmosphere. Throughout the modelling process, students verify compliance with circulation thresholds and accessibility guidelines to ensure realistic human movement.

activities.title: Asset Scaling & Circulation Clearance Modelling
activities.teacherDoes: Directs attention to the main projector. 'Watch as I insert a six-seat dining suite and an L-shaped modular sofa into this residential floor plan. Notice that when I drop the dining suite from the default library, the chairs clip the boundary wall, leaving only 520 mm of clearance. Under Australian Standard AS 1428.1, that breaches accessible circulation. Watch how I select the asset, lock proportional scaling, and use the digital caliper tool to set a clear 1000 mm primary walkway along the entrance and an 800 mm secondary passage between the dining chair perimeter and the wall. Notice how I verify the 850 mm arc clearance for the entry door swing to ensure wheelchair access is never impeded.'
activities.studentsDo: Track the modelled asset placement on the projector, cross-reference demonstrated clearance dimensions against the reference values in the workbook, and tick each compliant threshold in the audit table.
activities.visibleInstructions: Observe the asset placement and digital measuring routine on the main screen. Cross-reference the demonstrated clearances against your workbook table and tick each compliant threshold.
activities.questioning:
Why must we verify asset dimensions with a digital measuring tool rather than trusting visual estimation on screen? Expected: Digital screens lack physical depth perception and true 1:1 scale, making objects appear to fit when they actually breach physical clearance standards.
What operational issue occurs if a circulation corridor drops below 900 mm? Expected: It breaches AS 1428.1 compliance, impeding wheelchair mobility, pram access, and comfortable simultaneous passage for occupants.
How does locking proportional scaling protect the ergonomic integrity of 3D furniture assets? Expected: Non-proportional stretching distorts seat heights, table depths, and backrest angles, rendering the furniture functionally unviable for real humans.
activities.scaffolding:
Australian Standard AS 1428.1 Circulation Benchmarks:
- Primary entry and main circulation corridor: minimum 900–1000 mm
- Secondary walkways between seating / loose furniture: minimum 750–800 mm
- Internal door swing clearance arc: minimum 850 mm unobstructed
- Kitchen / joinery work triangle clearance: minimum 1000–1200 mm

activities.teacherDoes: Guides the class through synchronized placement: 'Open your Week 5 project file. Select the Asset Library tab and navigate to Built-In Joinery. Before releasing it into the scene, check your transform inspector in the bottom right panel: ensure Z-axis elevation is locked at exactly 0.00 mm so the cabinet sits flush on the slab. Watch my screen: when I snap the island into position, I switch to top-down orthographic view, select Tools > Dimension Caliper, click the outer benchtop edge, and pull a dimension line to the perimeter wall. We read 960 mm, which satisfies our 900 mm clearance criterion. If your gap reads under 900 mm, tap the arrow keys to nudge the island until it passes.'

activities.title: Digital Materiality & PBR Terminology
activities.teacherDoes: Presents four key physically-based rendering (PBR) texture concepts on the board: Diffuse/Albedo, Roughness, Specular Reflectivity, and Normal/Bump mapping. Compares a flat brown polygon with a high-resolution timber texture containing grain depth and variable matte/gloss reflectivity. Highlights how tactile cues generate warmth, visual weight, and acoustic perception in interior environments. Models how adjusting roughness from 0.1 to 0.9 transforms a surface from polished glass to matte stone.

activities.visibleInstructions: Match each PBR texture property in Column 1 with its correct technical definition from the bank below. Write the matching letter in the Match column.
activities.questioning:
What role does roughness play when rendering a polished marble countertop versus an unsealed timber dining table? Expected: Marble has low roughness causing sharp light reflections; unsealed timber has high roughness scattering light into a soft matte finish.
Why is bump or normal mapping essential in real-time VR rendering? Expected: It simulates 3D surface depth and tactile grooves without adding millions of polygons to the digital model.
Why must an Albedo (diffuse) texture map contain no baked lighting or shadow information? Expected: Baked lighting conflicts with dynamic in-engine light sources, creating unrealistic double shadows and incorrect exposure.
activities.scaffolding:
PBR Texture Property Definitions:
1. Diffuse / Albedo Map: Base colour and surface pattern without shadow or lighting calculations.
2. Roughness Channel: Micro-surface texture that controls light scatter between glossy and matte.
3. Specular Reflectivity: Quantity and sharpness of light mirrored off polished surface planes.
4. Normal / Bump Map: Simulated surface depth and structural relief that produces tactile shadows.

activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrates applying and scaling materials to architectural surfaces within the 3D interior tool. activities.questioning:
How does an oversized texture scale distort a client's perception when walking through a VR interior? Expected: It makes the room feel miniature or like a toy house because human eyes gauge spatial scale using expected material grain sizes.
Why should ceiling surfaces typically use high-roughness matte textures? Expected: To prevent distracting glare and specular reflections from artificial ceiling lights.
How does material visual weight affect spatial balance across an open-plan room? Expected: Heavy, dark, highly textured materials draw immediate focal attention and can make spaces feel enclosed, while light, smooth materials reflect light and expand perceived boundaries.
activities.scaffolding:
Word bank terms and concepts:
- UV scaling: Coordinate mapping system that sizes texture maps against real-world metric dimensions (e.g. 100 mm plank width)
- perceived scale: The cognitive sense of room volume deduced by comparing known material dimensions to human proportions
- visual weight: The visual prominence of an element based on texture, darkness, and contrast
- glare: Harsh, blinding reflections caused by low roughness or unmanaged specular highlights
- tactile cues: Visual suggestions of physical touch, grain, and warmth that evoke psychological comfort

activities.title: Layered Lighting Theory & Luminaire Configuration
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrates interior lighting principles on the projector within the 3D model. Explains the three mandatory lighting layers: Ambient (recessed downlights/diffused ceiling pendants for baseline visibility), Task (focused directional beams for reading, meal prep, or desk work), and Accent (wall-grazing, LED strip joinery lighting, artwork spotlights). Demonstrates configuring the Kelvin slider: 2700K (warm residential glow), 4000K (neutral task white), and 6000K (stark daylight). Models shadow casting settings to avoid dark virtual dead zones and illustrates how layered illumination eliminates harsh single-source shadows.
activities.studentsDo: Observe the teacher model the placement and intensity settings of each light type, recording the Kelvin values and layer classifications on their reference diagram.
activities.visibleInstructions: Observe the three lighting layers modelled on screen. Complete the table in your workbook by defining the functional purpose and target Kelvin range for ambient, task, and accent lighting.
activities.questioning:
Why is relying solely on central ambient ceiling lighting considered poor interior design practice? Expected: It creates flat, uninspiring illumination with harsh overhead shadows on user faces and work surfaces without functional focus.
What is the psychological effect of installing 5500K lighting in a residential living space? Expected: It feels sterile, clinical, and uninviting, disrupting relaxation and circadian rhythm.
Why should task lighting operate at a higher Kelvin temperature (3500K–4000K) than ambient lighting? Expected: Higher Kelvin neutral white improves visual contrast and acuity for focused work while reducing eye fatigue.
activities.scaffolding:
Lighting Layer Guidelines:
- Ambient: 300–400 lumens / 2700–3000K (warm, diffused general illumination)
- Task: 600–800 lumens / 3500–4000K (focused, glare-free directional work light)
- Accent: 200–300 lumens / 2700K (3:1 contrast ratio to highlight architectural focal points)

activities.title: Core Terminology and Qualitative Spatial Feedback
activities.teacherDoes: Welcome students to our empirical user testing unit. Today we examine how 1:1 virtual reality exposes spatial discrepancies that 2D floor plans hide. I will explicitly define our four core evaluation concepts on the board: perceptual scaling, ergonomic reach, sightline obstruction, and spatial volume. For example, consider this 2D plan of a kitchen: an island bench positioned 750 mm from a wall appears completely fine on paper with simple dimension lines. However, when you step into that same space at 1:1 scale in VR, the stereoscopic depth reveals that an adult cannot open the oven door without hitting the wall behind them. That is a perceptual discrepancy where 2D drafting masks an ergonomic reach and circulation failure. As I define each term, note the distinction between orthographic assumptions and stereoscopic reality.
activities.studentsDo: Record the formal architectural definitions for perceptual scaling, ergonomic reach, sightline obstruction, and spatial volume into the workbook table, referencing the teacher's modelled 2D versus 1:1 scale kitchen example.
activities.visibleInstructions: Complete the definition table in your workbook by writing out the full architectural definitions for the four core VR testing terms.
activities.questioning:
Why might a corridor width that looks adequate on a 2D plan feel uncomfortably narrow in virtual reality?
Expected: Orthographic plans lack vertical stereoscopic depth and human-scale presence, whereas VR simulates binocular vision and true ergonomic volume.

How does evaluating spatial volume in VR differ from reviewing an isometric 3D render?
Expected: Isometric renders provide an external bird's-eye view, whereas VR places the occupant inside the space at 1:1 eye height, conveying true volumetric compression or enclosure.
activities.scaffolding:
Core Architectural Definitions:
- Perceptual Scaling: How human observers judge room size, proportions, and ceiling height in an immersive space.
- Ergonomic Reach: The comfortable physical distance a user can extend their arms to access fixtures, joinery, and controls.
- Sightline Obstruction: Visual blockages caused by poorly placed partitions, cabinetry, or tall furniture.
- Spatial Volume: The three-dimensional cubic capacity of an interior space influencing perceived openness and enclosure.

activities.title: Structured Peer Usability Review Protocols
activities.teacherDoes: Let's unpack the peer review protocol required when testing interior architecture in virtual reality. Working in pairs, one student acts as the immersive Navigator inside the headset while the other acts as the Safety Observer and Recorder. I will model this setup now: as the observer, my first priority is safety—I verify that the navigator remains within the physical guardian boundary marked on the floor. On the casting monitor, I follow their live perspective as they walk through the entry zone. When the navigator reaches for an overhead cabinet, I observe their posture and log whether that fixture meets ergonomic reach standards. If they hesitate or turn sideways because a doorway feels tight, I record that spatial bottleneck on our testing rubric. Observers must record objective metric observations rather than vague impressions.

activities.title: Analysing Spatial Bottlenecks and Client Criteria
activities.teacherDoes: Look up at the case study on the board. We have a simulated VR testing scenario: during an immersive walkthrough of a coastal residence, the user navigates from the dining area into the kitchen and encounters a 700 mm pinch point between the kitchen island and the pantry joinery door. I will model how we structure an architectural analysis. First, describe the observed spatial conflict with precise dimensions: 'A 700 mm clear corridor between the fixed island and closed pantry unit.' Second, evaluate the client impact against the design brief and standards: 'This breaches AS 1428.1 universal accessibility guidelines requiring a minimum 900 mm continuous accessible path of travel, preventing independent wheelchair access and restricting two-person circulation.' Third, propose a measurable architectural remedy: 'Relocate the kitchen island 300 mm south towards the open living zone, achieving a 1000 mm clear thoroughfare while maintaining ergonomic bench-to-cooktop proximity.' activities.teacherDoes: Welcome to Lesson 2. Today we execute live 1:1 scale testing in our VR safety bays. Before anyone powers on a Meta Quest 3S headset, we must complete our mandatory workshop safety and hardware verification. Watch as I demonstrate with Bay 1: First, I physically inspect the taped floor perimeter to confirm a minimum 2-metre clear buffer free from chairs, bags, and trailing cords. Second, I demonstrate how to adjust the interpupillary distance (IPD) slider and tighten the rear head strap to prevent slippage and visual fatigue. Third, I cast the headset feed to our bay's secondary monitor, verifying that the screen mirrors head tracking with low latency. Fourth, the designated peer observer has their workbook rubric open on the desk. You must tick off all four items on your checklist before entering the guardian zone.

activities.title: Photometric Balance and Glare Diagnosis
activities.teacherDoes: The teacher introduces Iteration 2 objectives: refining surface materiality, balancing photometric lighting, and adjusting asset placement based on Week 6 empirical VR testing data. Directing student attention to the projection screen displaying the 3D render, the teacher models: 'Observe Callout 1 on the workstation desktop. Notice the harsh white reflection washing out the grain texture. In VisualizeR, the current surface roughness is set to 0.15, creating an uncomfortable specular highlight. When I increase the roughness slider to 0.65 and reduce the specular reflectance to 0.25, the light scatters diffusely across the timber, eliminating glare for the seated occupant. Now look at Callout 4 in the corridor: the illuminance drops below 100 lux, creating high visual contrast and an accessibility hazard under AS 1428.1. By adding a 500-lumen recessed downlight at 3000K, we achieve an even 300 lux transition.' The teacher systematically walks through callouts 1 to 4, demonstrating the diagnostic trigger, parameter value adjustment, and visual outcome for each.
activities.studentsDo: Examine the projected interior render and the corresponding Figure 1 diagram in your workbook. Annotate each of the four numbered callout regions by recording the observed lighting or material defect, the relevant photometric or material parameter, and the corrective Iteration 2 adjustment.

2. In Callout 1, diagnose the workstation desktop glare and specify the target roughness value.

4. In Callout 3, identify the overexposed window daylight balance and aperture correction.
5. In Callout 4, record the corridor shadow pooling and the luminaire adjustment required for AS 1428.1 safety.
activities.questioning:
Why does increasing a surface's roughness parameter from 0.15 to 0.65 diffuse specular glare without reducing the room's total illuminance? Expected: A higher roughness value introduces micro-surface irregularities that scatter reflected light rays across multiple angles rather than reflecting them parallel into the user's line of sight, softening highlights while preserving total ambient light energy.
How does unmitigated contrast between direct natural daylight (Callout 3) and unlit internal circulation (Callout 4) impact occupant visual fatigue? Expected: Extreme luminance ratios force the occupant's pupils to constantly adapt between high and low light levels, accelerating visual fatigue and compromising hazard perception during spatial transit.
activities.scaffolding:
Photometric & Material Reference Parameters:
- Specular Glare: Surface roughness < 0.20, high direct reflectance (> 0.70); creates harsh hotspots.
- Diffuse Matte: Surface roughness 0.60–0.80, low direct reflectance (< 0.30); scatters illumination evenly.
- Standard Lux Benchmarks (AS/NZS 1680):
  * General Circulation/Corridors: 100–150 lux minimum (recommend 200–300 lux for accessibility).
  * General Office/Living: 300–500 lux ambient.
  * Reading & Focused Task Work: 500–750 lux.
- Colour Temperature: Warm White = 3000K (residential/comfort), Neutral White = 4000K (commercial task), Cool Daylight = 5000K+ (causes clinical glare indoors).

activities.title: Architectural Communication & Cinematography Vocabulary
activities.teacherDoes: The teacher introduces key architectural communication and digital cinematography concepts: Eye-Level Panning, Spatial Sequence, Transitional Shot, and Focal Pause Point. Projecting a comparison video of professional architectural walkthroughs alongside amateur erratic VR footage, the teacher explains: 'Notice how the professional walkthrough fixes the camera height at 1550mm. This is Eye-Level Panning. If the camera floats at 2500mm, the client feels disoriented, like a floating drone, losing all sense of true ceiling height and ergonomic proportion. Next, notice how the camera moves from the entry threshold along the primary hallway into the lounge: that intentional pathway is our Spatial Sequence. As we transition between rooms, we use a smooth Transitional Shot at under 1.2 metres per second to avoid disorienting cuts. Finally, when the camera reaches the custom acoustic desk, it stops for 4 seconds—this is our Focal Pause Point, allowing the client to inspect material grain and joinery while the pitch script articulates its benefits.' The teacher instructs students to examine the scrambled definitions in their workbook bank.

What physiological problem occurs if a virtual camera accelerates rapidly or rotates on multiple axes simultaneously during a VR walkthrough? Expected: It creates sensory mismatch between the visual system and vestibular inner-ear balance, inducing nausea, dizziness, and simulator sickness.

Rule 3: Ensure collision boxes are active so the camera avoids geometric clipping through wall meshes—blank 3 is clipping. Rule 4: Structure navigation as an intentional spatial sequence from entry to destination. Finally, when showcasing your bespoke workstation, hold on a focal pause point for 3 to 5 seconds.'
