activities.title: Modeling Technical Justification Patterns
activities.teacherDoes: The teacher models how to construct a rigorous architectural justification using the three-part causal framework: 1. Evidence/Testing Observation ('VR user testing revealed...'), 2. Measurable Modification ('The desk offset was adjusted by 250mm and material roughness increased to 0.65...'), and 3. Client Success Criterion Alignment ('This guarantees compliance with AS 1428.1 accessibility and creates an inviting biophilic aesthetic'). The teacher dissects a weak script statement on the board: 'I moved the desk and changed the light bulb so the office feels nicer.' The teacher models rewriting it: 'During Week 6 VR testing, avatars collided with the central meeting table. In Iteration 2, the table was shifted 250mm along the X-axis and luminaire photometrics were adjusted to 500lm at 3200K. This satisfies AS 1428.1 with 1050mm clear pathways and eliminates specular glare to fulfill client wellness targets.'
activities.studentsDo: Analyse the teacher's modelled justification structure. In your workbook, deconstruct the sample paragraph by identifying its three causal elements and rewrite the flawed pitch sentence.
activities.visibleInstructions:
1. Look at the three-part justification framework modelled on the board.
2. In Section 1 of your workbook, label the Evidence, Modification, and Client Benefit in the sample paragraph.
3. In Section 2, rewrite the provided weak pitch sentence into a rigorous technical justification statement.
activities.questioning:
Why is subjective terminology like 'it looks modern' or 'it feels nice' insufficient in a professional architectural pitch? Expected: Subjective descriptions cannot be verified; clients and assessors require measurable criteria, Australian Standards compliance, and ergonomic rationale.
How does referencing empirical VR testing data strengthen your design credibility? Expected: It proves that your design modifications are responsive solutions to real human interactions rather than arbitrary stylistic choices.
activities.scaffolding: Three-Part Causal Framework displayed on slide: 1. Empirical Trigger: 'During 1:1 scale VR testing, peer feedback identified...'; 2. Technical Iteration: 'In response, Iteration 2 reconfigured [parameter/material/dimension] to...'; 3. Client Impact: 'This modification directly achieves Success Criterion [X] by enhancing...'.
activities.eLearning: Ensure student laptops remain closed while the justification framework is dissected.
activities.transition: Now that we know how to construct individual justification statements, let's map out the chronological structure of the entire pitch.

activities.title: Architectural Communication & Pitch Rubric Terminology
activities.teacherDoes: The teacher explicitly unpacks the Part 3 presentation rubric criteria, focusing on technical terminology and persuasive design justification strategies. The teacher models how to articulate a spatial decision using the 'Claim-Evidence-Reasoning' framework: 'Notice the difference in delivery standard. A weak presentation claims: "We made the hallway wider because it looked too tight." A high-standard presentation justifies: "In response to Week 6 user testing, corridor circulation was expanded from 820mm to 1050mm, satisfying AS 1428.1 continuous accessible paths of travel while maintaining acoustic buffer zoning between the collaboration hub and quiet focus rooms." Notice how precise metrics provide verifiable empirical evidence rather than subjective opinion. Today we master three foundational terms for our rubric: Photometric Balance, Spatial Zoning, and Ergonomic Clearance.' Display the three terms on the main screen and walk through how each connects to the GTMJ presentation rubric descriptors.

activities.questioning:
Why is using precise spatial terminology like '1050mm clearance' more persuasive to an architectural client than saying 'there is plenty of space'? Expected: Precise spatial terminology provides empirical evidence that accessibility standards (AS 1428.1) are satisfied rather than relying on subjective opinion.
How does defining spatial zoning strengthen the functional narrative of an interior walkthrough? Expected: It demonstrates that spaces have been grouped intentionally based on acoustics, occupant workflow, and privacy requirements.
activities.scaffolding:
Term Definitions and Presentation Framework:
- Photometric Balance: The proportional distribution of artificial and ambient light sources to eliminate glare and ensure visual comfort (target desktop illuminance 500 lux).
- Spatial Zoning: The architectural organisation of interior spaces according to functional usage, movement flow, and acoustic requirements.
- Ergonomic Clearance: The minimum physical dimensions required around fixtures to facilitate unhindered, accessible human movement to AS 1428.1 standards.
Sentence Starter: 'Our spatial zoning incorporates [feature] to ensure [clearance metric], achieving compliance with AS 1428.1 while balancing ambient illuminance at [lux level].'

activities.title: Walkthrough Pathing & Screencast Media Setup
activities.teacherDoes: The teacher models setting up the Meta Quest 3S screencast to local display hardware and demonstrates how to execute steady 1:1 scale camera movements along a pre-planned path: 'Watch my pacing through the reception zone. Rapid angular snapping causes disorientation for clients viewing a flat monitor. We set capture to 60fps to prevent judder, establish an eye-level camera height of 1500mm, and maintain a constant movement speed of 0.5 metres per second. When I reach the acoustic joinery, I pause for 4 seconds and deliver the synchronised justification: "Here, slatted timber panelling absorbs reverberant speech, maintaining an acoustic decay under 0.6 seconds." Notice how the spoken justification coincides with a stationary camera position.' The teacher highlights capture configuration, panning speed, and narration synchronisation on the teacher display.

activities.questioning:
How does rapid head movement during a VR screencast impact the client's viewing experience? Expected: Rapid head movement creates severe motion blur and visual disorientation for audience members viewing a 2D monitor.
Why is it essential to synchronise spoken commentary with designated visual pause points? Expected: Pausing the camera gives the viewer time to inspect the design feature visually while processing the spoken technical justification.
activities.scaffolding:
Recording Guidelines Summary:
- Motion: Smooth, linear panning without abrupt angular snapping.
- Frame Rate: Minimum 60fps to prevent video stuttering.
- Narration: Commentary synchronised to stationary 3–5 second visual pause points.
- Lighting: Photometric illuminance maps pre-rendered and verified.
- Scale: 1:1 scale eye-level perspective (1500mm height).
Word Bank: smooth, 60fps, commentary, lighting, 1:1 scale.

activities.title: Modelled Exemplar: Professional Client Presentation
activities.teacherDoes: The teacher models a high-standard 3-minute Virtual Pitch presentation using screencasted VR media: 'Observe how I open by connecting directly to our Yeppoon commercial client brief: "Our interior scheme resolves the primary brief constraint—providing flexible, accessible co-working spaces while reducing acoustic distraction." Then I transition to VR testing evidence: "During Week 6 immersion testing, our initial 820mm doorway created user navigation bottlenecks. We iterated by expanding this clearance to 1050mm compliant with AS 1428.1, eliminating collision boundaries." Finally, I justify finishes: "We specified acoustic blackbutt wall battens with recycled felt backing (NRC 0.85) to absorb reverberation, and balanced 3200K ambient luminaires with 500-lux task lighting to eliminate desktop glare." In your workbook, deconstruct these three structural movements.'
activities.studentsDo: Observe the teacher's modelled presentation on the main display. In your workbook, record the three key structural components of the presentation and identify how evidence was presented.
activities.visibleInstructions:
1. Watch the teacher's modelled 3-minute Virtual Pitch presentation.
2. In Section 1, note how the client brief connection was established.
3. In Section 2, record the empirical VR testing evidence cited.
4. In Section 3, identify the lighting and materiality justifications used.
activities.questioning:
How did the presenter transition smoothly from explaining spatial layout to justifying photometric lighting decisions? Expected: The presenter navigated into the secondary office zone and explicitly pointed out task lighting levels suited for desk work.
Why is it crucial to connect every spatial refinement back to the client persona during a pitch? Expected: It demonstrates that every design change serves the client's practical needs and comfort rather than designer whim.
activities.scaffolding:
Exemplar Presentation Structural Framework:
- Section 1 (Client Brief): Client persona, commercial purpose, accessibility constraints, regional coastal character.
- Section 2 (VR Iteration Evidence): Week 6 user testing collision bottlenecks, 820mm expanded to 1050mm, AS 1428.1 continuous accessible path.
- Section 3 (Materiality & Photometrics): Acoustic timber battens (NRC 0.85), indirect 3200K ambient coving, 500 lux task lighting, anti-glare finish.

activities.title: Summative Design Evaluation Methodology
activities.teacherDoes: The teacher presents the structure for formal summative design evaluation, demonstrating how to measure final outcomes against the quantitative and qualitative success criteria established in Week 2: 'In QCAA Design and Technologies, authentic evaluation requires objective, evidence-based appraisal rather than personal preference. Saying "the room feels welcoming" is subjective. Saying "the room achieves a continuous 1050mm accessible pathway, exceeding AS 1428.1, while task lighting delivers 520 lux at desk level" is an objective evaluation supported by empirical data. Furthermore, authentic design requires navigating design trade-offs. If we increased corridor width, did we compromise hot-desk capacity? Acknowledging trade-offs demonstrates sophisticated critical reflection.' The teacher contrasts subjective opinion with empirical evaluation on the main display.
activities.studentsDo: Listen to the presentation on evaluation methodology and complete the cloze passage in your workbook, selecting words from the provided word bank.
activities.visibleInstructions:
1. Follow the presentation on summative evaluation principles.
2. Complete sentences 1 through 3 in your cloze passage using the word bank.
3. Check that your answers correctly define measurable benchmarks and design trade-offs.
activities.questioning:
What is the critical difference between evaluating an aesthetic choice and evaluating an ergonomic clearance? Expected: Ergonomic clearances are evaluated quantitatively against physical measurements (AS 1428.1), whereas aesthetics are evaluated qualitatively against client mood boards and colour harmony.
Why must designers document design trade-offs rather than claiming their solution has zero flaws? Expected: Real-world built environment design always involves balancing competing priorities like budget, spatial volume, and material properties; documenting trade-offs demonstrates authentic critical evaluation.
activities.scaffolding:
Evaluation Methodology Concepts:
- Measurable Benchmarks: Pre-established quantitative targets (e.g. 1050mm clearance, 500 lux illuminance, 0.6s reverberation time).
- Empirical Evidence: Verifiable physical data and testing observations recorded during 1:1 scale VR walkthroughs.
- Design Trade-offs: Conscious compromises made between competing constraints (e.g. sacrificing desk density to achieve universal wheelchair access).
Word Bank: measurable, empirical, trade-offs.

workbookSpec.title: Summative Evaluation Principles Cloze Passage
workbookSpec.prompt: Complete the cloze passage using the terms from the word bank to define the principles of summative design appraisal.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: 1: measurable, 2: empirical, 3: trade-offs
workbookSpec.text: Formal summative evaluation requires designers to appraise their final solution against {{1}} benchmarks established in the initial design brief. Rather than relying on subjective preference, ergonomic compliance must be verified through {{2}} spatial measurements aligned with Australian Standards. When evaluating aesthetic outcomes, designers contrast rendered solutions against the client mood board to verify visual cohesion. Any design compromises made between cost, aesthetics, and circulation must be documented through a balanced analysis of design {{3}}.

activities.teacherAnswerKey:
{{1}} measurable — Pre-determined quantitative and qualitative targets from the Week 2 brief.
{{2}} empirical — Verifiable physical data and testing observations rather than subjective opinion.
{{3}} trade-offs — Rationalised compromises between competing constraints such as cost, spatial volume, and material specifications.

activities.title: Success Criteria Audit & Solution Appraisal
activities.teacherDoes: The teacher guides students through appraising their final virtual interior against their Week 2 measurable design criteria: 'Open your folios to your initial Week 2 criteria table. You defined targets for circulation, accessibility, lighting, and materiality. In your workbook continuum scale, rate your final outcome from 1 (Criterion Not Satisfied) to 5 (Criterion Fully Exceeded). Watch how I model a score of 5: "The final interior achieves a rating of 5 because empirical VR measurements confirm a continuous 1070mm pathway throughout circulation zones, exceeding AS 1428.1. While expanding this path required reducing hot desks from eight to six, this trade-off prioritised universal accessibility in accordance with client criteria." Substantiate your score with exact dimensions and trade-off analysis.'
activities.studentsDo: Evaluate your final interior design solution against your initial success criteria. Mark your rating on the continuum scale in your workbook and write a structured justification justifying your score with quantitative evidence.
activities.visibleInstructions:
1. Review the initial ergonomics and spatial criteria established in Week 2.
2. Mark your rating on the 1-to-5 continuum scale in your workbook.
3. Write a justification citing exact millimetre clearances and movement observations to support your rating.
activities.questioning:
If a design achieved high aesthetic appeal but compromised corridor width to 850mm, what rating and justification should be assigned? Expected: A rating of 2 or 3, acknowledging aesthetic success while identifying non-compliance with the 900mm AS 1428.1 benchmark.
What quantitative evidence best proves that your lighting design meets commercial standards? Expected: Citing measured lux levels (e.g. 500 lux at desktop, 300 lux in general circulation) and correlated Kelvin colour temperatures.
activities.scaffolding:
Continuum Rating Scale:
1 = Criterion Not Satisfied (critical spatial or accessibility non-compliance)
2 = Partially Satisfied (major compromises, substandard dimensions)
3 = Satisfied (satisfies baseline standard, 900mm clear paths)
4 = Exceeded (1000mm+ clearances, balanced photometrics, verified in VR)
5 = Fully Exceeded (exemplary universal access to AS 1428.1, optimal lux levels, seamless client brief alignment)
Sentence Starter: 'The final design achieves a rating of [4/5] because empirical measurements confirm [clearance in mm / lux level], satisfying [standard/brief]. Although [trade-off compromise], this was justified because [client priority].'

activities.title: Comparative Appraisal: 2D Drafting vs. 1:1 Scale VR Prototyping
activities.teacherDoes: The teacher leads a comparative synthesis discussing traditional 2D CAD drafting versus 1:1 scale immersive VR prototyping: 'Consider how both tools served your design workflow. 2D CAD drafting is universally understood, produces precise dimensioned blueprints, and is essential for council approvals and trade contractors. However, it cannot convey spatial volume or human emotional response. In contrast, 1:1 scale VR immersion lets you experience spatial volume directly, identifying low bulkheads, glare, and ergonomic pinch points early. In the middle, both tools translate client briefs, define spatial boundaries, and record iterative modifications. In your workbook overlap diagram, synthesise these unique strengths and common capabilities.'
activities.studentsDo: Complete the comparative overlap diagram in your workbook, recording unique benefits of 2D CAD drafting, unique benefits of 1:1 scale VR prototyping, and shared design capabilities.
activities.visibleInstructions:
1. In Region 1, record the unique capabilities of traditional 2D CAD drafting.
2. In Region 2, record shared design capabilities common to both media.
3. In Region 3, record unique spatial advantages offered by 1:1 scale VR prototyping.
activities.questioning:
Which spatial flaws are almost impossible to detect in 2D floor plans but become immediately obvious in 1:1 scale VR immersion? Expected: Vertical clearance issues, sightline obstructions, feeling cramped under low bulkheads, and visual glare from unshielded fixtures.
Why is 2D CAD drafting still an indispensable tool in architectural practice alongside VR? Expected: 2D drafting provides precise dimensional blueprints, structural documentation, and universal notation required for construction and regulatory compliance.
activities.scaffolding:
Overlap Diagram Synthesis Framework:
- Left (Traditional 2D CAD Drafting Only): Standard orthographic blueprints (plans, sections, elevations); universal contractor conventions; low hardware computing overhead; legal council submission format.
- Middle (Shared Capabilities): Spatial boundary definition; wall partition layout planning; client brief interpretation; iterative design modification tracking.
- Right (1:1 Scale Immersive VR Prototyping Only): True stereoscopic depth perception; immediate real-time ergonomic clearance testing; dynamic photometric lighting and glare simulation; empathetic spatial experience at human scale.
